meaning: In a way that makes you very annoyed or frustrated
hindi: बेहद झुंझलाहट से, खिजाने वाले ढंग से
trick: MADDENING = making you MAD; + -LY = in a mad-making way.
examples: My middle school years were maddeningly confusing and roundabout.
The bus was maddeningly slow today.

meaning: A bright purplish-red or pink colour
trick: MAGENTA = MAGic pink: the bright ink colour in printers.
examples: The green tablecloth had little magenta stars on it.
She painted her nails a bright magenta.

meaning: Worthless, low people (used as an insult, here about themselves); also small worm-like young of flies found in rotting food
trick: MAGGOTS crawl in GARBAGE: the lowest of the low.
examples: We were all maggots reborn, starting at zero.
There were maggots in the rotten meat.

usage.pattern: feel like maggots / maggots in something

meaning: Generous and kind, especially towards someone weaker or a rival
trick: MAGNA = great + ANIMUS = spirit: a great-spirited person.
examples: He held out a stick of gum to Aziza with a stiff, magnanimous air.
She was magnanimous in victory and praised her opponent.

usage.pattern: be magnanimous (to/towards someone) / magnanimous in victory

meaning: Became bigger or stronger; also made something look larger, as with a lens
hindi: बढ़ गया, बढ़ा; बड़ा करके दिखाया
trick: MAGNIFYING glass makes things big: the fear grew big too.
examples: With each gulp of sea water, my fear magnified.
Her worries magnified when he didn't call.

meaning: A tall tropical tree with hard reddish-brown wood used for fine furniture
trick: MAHOGANY = MAHAl-quality wood: rich furniture for palaces.
examples: We took shelter beneath tall mahogany trees in the jungle.
My grandfather has a mahogany table in the dining room.

meaning: To manage to see, hear or understand something that is not clear; also (informal) to kiss
trick: MAKE OUT the shape: your eyes 'make' it come 'out' of the blur.
examples: Laila could make out people in bright tunics on the roofs.
I couldn't make out what he was saying on the phone.

usage.pattern: make out something / make something out

meaning: Made quickly from whatever is available, to use for a short time
trick: MAKE a SHIFT: make something to shift by for now.
examples: She pictured plastic sheets tied to makeshift poles in a refugee camp.
We used a box as a makeshift table.

meaning: Failing to work in the normal or correct way
hindi: ठीक से काम न करना, खराब होना
trick: MAL = bad + FUNCTIONING: functioning badly.
examples: The projector has been malfunctioning recently.
The traffic lights were malfunctioning all morning.

meaning: The desire to hurt or upset someone
trick: MALICE = MAL (bad) + ICE in the heart.
examples: They looked harmless, as if they didn't bear any malice.
I said it as a joke, without any malice.

usage.pattern: bear malice / without malice / malice towards someone

meaning: Meaning to hurt or upset someone on purpose
trick: MALICIOUS = full of MALICE (bad intent).
examples: She knew that Hasina wasn't malicious.
He spread malicious rumours about his boss.

meaning: (of a tumour) cancerous and likely to spread; also wanting to do great harm, evil
trick: MALIGN = bad; a MALIGNANT tumour does bad and spreads.
examples: They weren't even tumors, much less malignant.
The doctor said the lump was not malignant.

meaning: A strong wish to do harm; great evil
trick: Same root as MALIGNANT: MAL = bad, so MALIGNITY = badness at heart.
examples: In sheer malignity, this traitor crept in at night and destroyed our work.
She was shocked by the malignity of his words.

usage.pattern: in (sheer) malignity / the malignity of something

meaning: Easily changed or influenced; also (of metal) able to be hammered into shape
trick: MALLET hits metal into shape: MALLEABLE things bend to the mallet.
examples: Our beliefs are malleable, and our memories are unreliable.
Young children's minds are very malleable.

meaning: Treating a person or animal badly or cruelly
trick: MAL = bad + TREATING: treating badly.
examples: They were used to thrashing and maltreating the animals as they chose.
He was arrested for maltreating his dog.

meaning: An official order or authority to do a particular job
trick: MANDATE = a MAN's DATE with duty: the job he's been officially given.
examples: The project was founded with a mandate to improve the teaching of negotiation.
The new government has a mandate to fight corruption.

usage.pattern: a mandate to do something / a mandate for something

meaning: A small musical instrument like a lute, with a round back and pairs of metal strings
trick: MANDOLIN sounds like a little MANDOLINE-shaped guitar from Italy.
examples: He had a pink birthmark shaped like an upside-down mandolin.
My uncle plays the mandolin at weddings.

meaning: The long thick hair on the neck of a horse or lion
trick: MANE is the MAIN hair on a horse's neck.
examples: Jalil just kept brushing his horse's mane.
The lion shook its golden mane.

meaning: Moved carefully and skilfully through a tight or difficult space (US spelling; British 'manoeuvred')
trick: MAN-EUVER: a MAN steering his way through.
examples: I maneuvered through the wind tunnel to take my place.
She maneuvered the car into the tiny parking space.

usage.pattern: maneuver through / into / around something; maneuver something into something

meaning: Badly crushed, twisted or torn so it is hard to recognise
trick: MANGLED = MANGO through a grinder: crushed beyond shape.
examples: The streets were full of the burnt, mangled shells of cars.
The bicycle was mangled in the accident.

meaning: (of lawns or gardens) cut and kept very neat; (of hands) with nails carefully cared for
trick: MANI = hand (manicure); a MANICURED lawn gets the same fussy care.
examples: There are manicured lawns, palm trees, and shade trees.
She has beautifully manicured nails.

meaning: Something wonderful that comes when you badly need it (from the food God gave in the Bible)
trick: 'MANNA from heaven': food that fell from the sky for hungry travellers.
examples: That pizza tasted like manna from heaven.
For the starving villagers, the food aid was manna from heaven.

meaning: A life-size model of a human body, used to show clothes or for training
trick: MANNEQUIN = a fake MAN in the shop window.
examples: My hand looked more like a mannequin's than something human.
The mannequin in the window was wearing a red dress.

meaning: Having good manners; polite
trick: MANNER-LY = full of good MANNERS.
examples: When Jalil visited, Nana was quiet and mannerly.
He was a mannerly young man who always said thank you.

meaning: A skilful or planned movement, especially by soldiers in a fight (British spelling; US 'maneuver')
trick: MAN-OEUVRE: from French 'main' (hand) + 'oeuvre' (work): handwork, a skilful move.
examples: This was only a light skirmishing manoeuvre to create a little disorder.
Parking in that tight spot was a tricky manoeuvre.

usage.pattern: a + adjective + manoeuvre / carry out a manoeuvre

meaning: Substances such as animal dung or chemicals put on soil to help crops grow
trick: MANURE comes from MANual work spreading dung on fields.
examples: Later there would be need for seeds and artificial manures.
Farmers buy different manures for their fields.

meaning: (informal, in the phrase 'lose your ...') your mind or sanity; also small glass balls used in a children's game
trick: 'Lost his MARBLES': the little balls of sense rolled out of his head.
examples: He totally loses his marbles and does something terrible.
My grandad is ninety but he still has all his marbles.

usage.pattern: lose your marbles / have all your marbles

meaning: Cocktails made with tequila, lime juice and orange liqueur, often served with salt on the glass rim
trick: MARGARITA = a girl's name for a salty-rimmed lime drink.
examples: We had margaritas, and he told me all about it.
They ordered two margaritas at the beach bar.

meaning: Treated as unimportant and kept outside the main group in society (US spelling; British 'marginalised')
trick: MARGIN = the edge of the page: MARGINALIZED people are pushed to the edge.
examples: He grew up marginalized like me and wasn't supposed to amount to much.
The new scheme helps marginalized communities.

meaning: Plants with bright orange or yellow flowers
trick: MARIGOLDS are GOLD-coloured flowers (genda in every garland).
examples: In the centre of the table was a vase of fresh marigolds.
She made a garland of marigolds for the puja.

meaning: A harbour for small boats, yachts and pleasure boats
trick: MARINA = MARINE (sea) + a place to park boats.
examples: Tourists come to see San Diego's stunning marina.
We walked along the marina and looked at the yachts.

meaning: Skill at shooting accurately at a target
trick: A MARKSMAN hits the MARK: MARKSMANSHIP is his skill.
examples: The militiamen sharpened their marksmanship in the mountains.
The soldier won a medal for marksmanship.

meaning: A jam made from oranges or other citrus fruit (here from carrots)
trick: MARMALADE: MA MADE orange jam for toast.
examples: On the sill were jars in which she made carrot marmalade.
I like marmalade on my toast.

meaning: To gather and arrange things (such as thoughts or facts) in a clear order; also (noun) an official who keeps order at events
trick: An army MARSHAL lines up troops: you MARSHAL your thoughts into line.
examples: He tried hard to marshal his thoughts, but could think of nothing to say.
She took a moment to marshal her arguments before the meeting.

meaning: Areas of soft, wet, low land
trick: MARSH + LANDS = squelchy wet lands.
examples: There were paintings of them wading in lagoons and sunbathing in marshlands.
Many birds live in the marshlands near the river.

meaning: People who are killed or suffer because of their religious or political beliefs
trick: MARTYRS are shaheed: remembered with MARTYRS' day.
examples: And now they're both shaheed, my boys, both martyrs.
The country honours its martyrs every year.

usage.pattern: die as martyrs / be remembered as martyrs

meaning: To feel great surprise and admiration at something
trick: MARVEL comics: full of things that make you MARVEL.
examples: Not one of the animals ever ceased to marvel at that.
We marvel at how fast children learn.

meaning: Felt great surprise and admiration (US spelling; British 'marvelled')
trick: MARVEL + ED: she was amazed, past tense.
examples: She marveled at the sweet, lovely texture of it.
The tourists marveled at the size of the temple.

meaning: Feeling great surprise and admiration (US spelling; British 'marvelling')
hindi: चकित होते हुए, आश्चर्य करते हुए
trick: MARVEL + ING: still amazed while doing something.
examples: They were marveling at the baby's light hair and pink cheeks.
We stood there marveling at the sunset.

meaning: Make-up put on the eyelashes to make them look darker and thicker
trick: MASCARA makes your lashes look like a MASK of black.
examples: Tears of shame mixed with soapy water, rouge, and mascara.
Her mascara ran when she cried.

meaning: A soft mix of grain and water fed to animals; also any food crushed into a soft mass
trick: MASH = everything MASHED together in a bucket for the hens.
examples: Jones used sometimes to mix some of it in our mash, said one of the hens.
The farmer gave the pigs a bucket of warm mash.

usage.pattern: feed animals mash / a bucket of mash

meaning: Pressing (buttons or keys) hard and repeatedly; also crushing food into a soft mass
trick: MASHING buttons like MASHING potatoes: smash, smash, smash.
examples: People start mashing buttons at random until the light comes on.
He kept mashing the lift button, but it didn't come.

meaning: Enjoying or seeking things that cause you pain or suffering
trick: MASOCHISM: named after Mr. Sacher-MASOCH, who wrote about loving pain.
examples: Staying in that training seemed like masochism.
Running a marathon in this heat is pure masochism.

usage.pattern: pure masochism / a form of masochism

meaning: A person who seems to enjoy pain, hardship or suffering
trick: MASOCHIST: a person who practises MASOCHISM.
examples: I was a self-made masochist from the Indiana cornfields.
You must be a masochist to wake up at 4 a.m. every day.

meaning: Seeming to enjoy pain or suffering
trick: MASOCHIST + IC: describing someone who loves pain.
examples: Lifting weights the night before a race would impress that masochistic man.
He has a masochistic love of cold showers.

meaning: (before 'jar') a glass jar with a screw lid, used for storing food; also a person who builds with stone
trick: Mr. John MASON invented the screw-top glass jar.
examples: Then I remembered that we had two mason jars filled with coins.
She keeps her pickles in a mason jar.

meaning: To pretend to be someone or something you are not; also (noun) a party where people wear masks
hindi: ढोंग करना, भेष बदलना; नकाबपोश नाच
trick: MASQUERADE = behind a MASK: pretending to be someone else.
examples: He knew her language well enough to masquerade as a believer.
The thief masqueraded as a delivery man.

meaning: The top of a ship's mast or a flagpole; also the name printed at the top of a newspaper
trick: MAST + HEAD = the head (top) of the mast.
examples: They saw the green flag fluttering at the masthead.
The flag flew proudly from the masthead.

meaning: To appear suddenly or come into view; also to happen as hoped (US spelling; British 'materialise')
trick: MATERIAL-IZE: become solid material, out of thin air.
examples: Seeing images from that race materialize on my screen thrilled me.
A taxi seemed to materialize out of nowhere.

meaning: Appearing or coming into view, often suddenly
trick: MATERIALIZING: turning into MATERIAL right before your eyes.
examples: Mariam found people materializing from the rubble and moving into the streets.
Dark clouds were materializing on the horizon.

meaning: An afternoon showing of a film or play
trick: MATIN = morning in French; a MATINEE is the early (daytime) show.
examples: We saw a matinee at the cinema where a comedy was showing.
Matinee tickets are cheaper than the evening show.

usage.pattern: a matinee (show) / go to a matinee

meaning: A dignified, middle-aged married woman (old-fashioned); also a senior nurse in a hospital
trick: MATRON from MATER = mother: a motherly older woman.
examples: She sat between a small old woman and a fat matron without a hat.
The matron ordered the visitors to leave the ward.

meaning: Small pieces of thick material put on the floor
trick: MATS lie flat on the floor: you MAT-ter little, you just get stepped on.
examples: The hallway smelt of boiled cabbage and old rag mats.
Please wipe your feet on the mats.

meaning: A flat, non-shiny black colour
trick: MATTE = not shiny (opposite of gloss), like a MAT on the floor.
examples: It was painted matte black and wrapped with white tape.
He bought a phone with a matte black finish.

usage.pattern: painted matte black / a matte black + noun

meaning: (of hair or fur) tangled into a thick, sticky mass
trick: MATTED hair is like a MAT: woven tight and stuck.
examples: Her hair was matted with sweat.
The stray dog's fur was matted with mud.

usage.pattern: be matted with something / matted + noun

meaning: (usually after 'as a') as the normal or expected thing, without thinking twice
trick: Of COURSE! It's a MATTER OF COURSE: obvious, routine.
examples: The animals had assumed as a matter of course that these would be shared equally.
She checks her emails every morning as a matter of course.

partners: do something as a matter of course

meaning: People who think and act differently from others; nonconformists
hindi: लीक से हटकर चलने वाले, स्वतंत्र विचारक
trick: MAVERICK = an unbranded calf that ran free (and Tom Cruise's call sign).
examples: People call themselves experts, innovators and mavericks without real experience.
Tech is full of mavericks who break the rules.

meaning: (informal) used up completely, to the highest limit (e.g. a credit card)
hindi: पूरी तरह खत्म, हद तक इस्तेमाल (बोलचाल)
trick: MAX-ED OUT = hit the MAXimum; nothing left.
examples: Meanwhile, our credit cards are maxed out.
My phone storage is maxed out again.

usage.pattern: be maxed out / max out something

meaning: A short statement of a general truth or rule for behaviour
trick: MAXIM = MAXimum wisdom in minimum words.
examples: The Commandments could be reduced to a single maxim: Four legs good, two legs bad.
My father's maxim was 'Honesty is the best policy.'

usage.pattern: a maxim / the old maxim that ...

meaning: A confusing network of paths or streets where it is easy to get lost
trick: MAZE amazes you: you get lost in it.
examples: The city had a maze of narrow streets.
We got lost in the maze of lanes in the old city.

meaning: Very small in amount and not enough (US spelling; British 'meagre')
trick: MEAGER = MEAGRE eager: eager for more because there's so little.
examples: I showed her my meager stash of energy gels.
He lived on a meager salary.

meaning: The state of being very small, thin or too little (British spelling)
trick: MEAGRE + NESS = the quality of being meagre.
examples: The meagreness of his body was only emphasized by the blue overalls.
The meagreness of the meal disappointed the guests.

meaning: Following a winding, curving path, not a straight line
trick: Like the river MAEANDER in Turkey, famous for its bends.
examples: I swam a meandering line that stretched to seven and a half miles.
A meandering stream ran through the village.

meaning: An infectious disease that causes fever and small red spots on the skin
trick: MEASLES = spots you can't MEASURE: so many red dots.
examples: Every rash was either chicken pox or measles.
The child was vaccinated against measles.

meaning: (informal) very small, thin or not enough; disappointingly little
trick: MEASLY: as small and pathetic as a MEASLES spot.
examples: They were all shivering in their measly poncho liners.
He gave me a measly ten rupees.

meaning: On the inner side of the body, nearer the middle line
trick: MEDIAL = toward the MEDIAN (middle) line of the body.
examples: Each time my medial tendon twinged, it felt like a raw nerve.
He injured the medial ligament in his knee.

meaning: Very cruel, harsh or old-fashioned (informal); also from the Middle Ages (about 500–1500 AD)
trick: MEDI-EVAL = middle ages: torture rooms of old castles feel medieval.
examples: It's medieval, and it comes at you fast in the third week of training.
The punishment at that old school was medieval.

usage.pattern: something is medieval / a medieval + noun

meaning: The state of being only average or ordinary, not very good
trick: MEDIOCRE = 'middle of the rock' – stuck halfway up, never at the top.
examples: It may be satisfactory, but that's another word for mediocrity.
Don't settle for mediocrity when you can do better.

usage.pattern: settle for mediocrity / a sea of mediocrity

meaning: Quiet, gentle and too ready to obey or accept things without protest
trick: MEEK sounds like a mouse's 'squeak' – small and quiet.
examples: There was no room for any response but meek gratitude.
The meek boy never argued with his teacher.

meaning: More quiet, humble or timid; less forceful
trick: MEEK + ER = even more meek.
examples: "I don't know what you're talking about," I said, sounding far meeker than I'd like.
Her voice grew meeker when the boss walked in.

meaning: In a quiet, humble way, obeying without arguing
trick: MEEK + LY: acting like a meek mouse.
examples: Zalmai meekly let himself be led upstairs.
He meekly said sorry and sat down.

meaning: Deep, long-lasting sadness; sad and gloomy
trick: MELAN = black (melanin): 'black bile' was once thought to cause sadness.
examples: It was an allegory about the melancholy fate of the Russian revolution.
The rainy evening put her in a melancholy mood.

meaning: A confused, noisy fight or crowd of people pushing together
trick: MELEE sounds like 'mela' – a crowded, messy fair.
examples: There was a melee in the yard.
My phone was lost in the melee after the concert.

usage.pattern: a melee of people / in the melee

meaning: Soft, warm and gentle (of light, sound or mood); also relaxed and calm
trick: MELLOW sounds like 'marshmallow' – soft and sweet.
examples: The whole room was flooded with a pleasant, mellow light.
He became more mellow as he got older.

meaning: A story or behaviour full of exaggerated emotion and dramatic events
trick: MELO (song) + DRAMA: drama with background music to make you cry.
examples: It's a heartfelt saga full of romance and melodrama.
Stop the melodrama; it's only a small scratch.

usage.pattern: full of melodrama / a bit of melodrama

meaning: Showing feelings in a much more extreme way than needed
trick: MELODRAMA + TIC: acting like a TV soap star.
examples: Laughter in the pain turned the whole melodramatic experience upside down.
Don't be so melodramatic about a broken pencil.

meaning: A large round fruit with a hard skin and sweet, juicy flesh inside
trick: MELON rhymes with 'lemon' but is much bigger and sweeter.
examples: She misses the melon hawkers in Karteh-Parwan.
We ate a cold melon on a hot afternoon.

meaning: Official notes or short written messages within an office (plural of 'memorandum')
trick: MEMO-RANDA = many memos; they help you remember (memory).
examples: The pigs worked hard on files, reports, minutes and memoranda.
The manager sent two memoranda about the new rules.

meaning: A person or thing that is a danger or threat; a threatening quality
trick: MENACE sounds like 'Dennis the Menace' – always causing trouble.
examples: He made himself more upright, taking on an air of menace.
Stray dogs have become a menace in our street.

usage.pattern: a menace to someone/something / an air of menace

meaning: Looking or sounding as if it will cause harm
trick: MENACE + ING: something that menaces you.
examples: The dogs let out deep, menacing growls, and the pigs fell silent.
A menacing dark cloud hung over the village.

meaning: Boring, low-status work that needs little skill
trick: MENIAL = jobs for 'many-al' – any person could do it.
examples: Doing even the most menial of tasks made the larger tasks seem easier.
He did menial jobs like washing dishes to pay rent.

meaning: A serious illness in which the covering of the brain and spinal cord becomes inflamed
trick: MENINGES (brain covering) + ITIS (swelling).
examples: Some doctors believe toxic stress harms kids more than polio or meningitis.
The baby was given a vaccine against meningitis.

meaning: Soldiers who fight for any country or group that pays them
trick: MERCENARY ~ 'mercy for money': they fight for whoever pays.
examples: Our techniques clearly worked with mercenaries and terrorists.
The king hired mercenaries to protect his castle.

meaning: Only; nothing more than
trick: MERELY = 'mere' + ly: a mere thing, nothing more.
examples: She merely shook her head and went on sobbing.
I was merely asking a question.

meaning: Combines or joins together to become one
hindi: मिल जाता है, विलय होता है
trick: MERGE = two lanes merge into one road.
examples: All of that ripples out, merges, and multiplies within our society.
The small stream merges with the river near the bridge.

meaning: A system where people get power or success because of their ability, not money or family
trick: MERIT + -CRACY (rule): the best performers rule.
examples: The military likes to think of itself as a pure meritocracy.
A true meritocracy rewards hard work and talent.

meaning: Happy fun and laughter
trick: MERRY + MENT: the feeling of a merry Christmas.
examples: Her voice was shrill with merriment.
The party was full of music and merriment.

meaning: The state of being cheerful and full of fun
trick: MERRY + NESS: the quality of being merry.
examples: She imagined the air in Herat crackling with merriness.
The merriness of the children filled the house.

meaning: Cheerful and full of fun; (of a group) jolly or carefree
trick: MERRY Christmas – the happiest time of year.
examples: He skipped round, whisking his tail with a merry laugh.
We had a merry time at the wedding.

meaning: Material like a net made of threads or wires with small holes
trick: MESH = MESSY net of crossed threads.
examples: It was strange seeing the world through a mesh screen.
The window has a wire mesh to keep out mosquitoes.

usage.pattern: a mesh + noun / through a mesh

meaning: So beautiful or interesting that you cannot stop looking (US spelling; British 'mesmerising')
trick: MESMER was a doctor who 'hypnotised' people.
examples: The cliff at the Cape of Good Hope is beautiful and mesmerizing.
The dancer's moves were mesmerizing.

usage.pattern: something is mesmerizing / a mesmerizing + noun

meaning: A complete change of form or character, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly
trick: META (change) + MORPH (shape): the shape changes.
examples: Whatever is in front of you becomes fuel for your metamorphosis.
His metamorphosis from a shy boy to a confident speaker amazed us.

usage.pattern: a metamorphosis from something to/into something

meaning: A way of describing something by calling it something else (e.g. 'life is a journey'); a symbol
trick: META (beyond) + PHOR (carry): carries meaning beyond the words.
examples: It was the perfect metaphor for my twisted life.
'Time is money' is a common metaphor.

meaning: Gave out a punishment or justice (always followed by 'out')
trick: METED out = MEASURED out, like a meter.
examples: He hoped justice would be meted out without delay.
Harsh punishment was meted out to the thieves.

meaning: Short for methamphetamine, a strong illegal drug (informal)
trick: METH = short for METHamphetamine.
examples: His son was caught using meth in the bathroom.
Meth can destroy a person's health very quickly.

meaning: A person addicted to the drug meth (rude slang)
trick: METH + HEAD: someone whose head is full of meth.
examples: You end up sweating like a meth-head for thirty minutes on an elliptical.
The film showed a meth-head living on the street.

meaning: Done carefully, step by step, in a fixed order
trick: METHOD + ICAL: always following a method.
examples: To Laila, the sounds were those of a methodical, familiar proceeding.
She is very methodical and checks every detail.

usage.pattern: be methodical about something / a methodical + noun

meaning: Giving great attention to every small detail
trick: METICULOUS sounds like 'meter-culous' – measuring every millimetre.
examples: She was still ticking off items with the same meticulous attention.
He is meticulous about keeping his desk clean.

meaning: In a very careful way, paying attention to every small detail
trick: METICULOUS + LY: done like a careful watchmaker.
examples: He hid behind a meticulously constructed false display of confidence.
She meticulously checked every page for mistakes.

meaning: A way of measuring or judging something; also relating to the metre system
trick: METRIC = METER: a scale to measure things.
examples: Making money, by itself, was a lousy metric for myself.
Happiness is a better metric of success than salary.

meaning: Cried weakly like a kitten; spoke in a whiny voice
trick: MEW = a kitten's cry; MEWLED = cried like one.
examples: "What's the matter?" he mewled, mimicking her.
The hungry kitten mewled at the door.

meaning: Crying weakly, like a kitten or a small baby
trick: MEW-ling = making kitten 'mew' sounds.
examples: She kept mewling and shivering as she rubbed her face.
A mewling baby woke up the whole house.

meaning: The middle of something (place, time or situation)
trick: MIDST = MIDdle + ST.
examples: If you're in the midst of a crisis, everything can feel meaningless.
She called me in the midst of my exam.

meaning: Great strength or power
trick: MIGHT = MIGHTY: with all your might = with full power.
examples: Boxer tried with all his might to remember what came next.
He pushed the car with all his might.

meaning: Very (informal, mainly US); also very strong or powerful
trick: MIGHTY = full of might: 'mighty quick' = very quick.
examples: He said she'd have to be buried mighty quickly because of the heat.
That soup smells mighty good.

meaning: Slightly; not very much
trick: MILD + LY: a mild amount, like mild chilli.
examples: It's the mildly dissatisfied creature that will work hardest to survive.
I was mildly surprised by the news.

meaning: A group of ordinary people trained to fight like soldiers, not part of the regular army
trick: MILITIA = MILITary + militia: an army of ordinary people.
examples: It was four men against a well-armed militia of 30 to 200 men.
The village formed a militia to protect itself.

usage.pattern: a militia of + people / join a militia
